title: ALB versus NLB versus GWLB
hook: Elastic Load Balancing offers three load balancer types for different layers: Application Load Balancer (ALB) for HTTP at Layer 7, Network Load Balancer (NLB) for TCP/UDP at Layer 4 with static IPs, and Gateway Load Balancer (GWLB) for transparent inline inspection at Layer 3.

blocks.text: ALB terminates HTTP/HTTPS, supports path/host/header routing, WebSocket, and AWS WAF integration — default for web APIs and microservices. NLB preserves source IP, handles millions of requests per second, offers static Elastic IP per AZ — used for TCP, PrivateLink targets, and extreme performance. GWLB uses GENEVE encapsulation to steer traffic through third-party firewall appliances without changing routing tables on workloads.

entries.plainDefinition: Layer 7 load balancer for HTTP/HTTPS with content-based routing.
Layer 4 load balancer with ultra-low latency and static IP support.
entries.example: TCP 5432 to RDS proxy targets; PrivateLink provider NLB.

entries.plainDefinition: Layer 3 transparent bump-in-the-wire for inspection appliances.
entries.example: Traffic via GWLB endpoint to firewall fleet then to app subnet.

entries.plainDefinition: Set of registered targets (IP, instance, Lambda) receiving balanced traffic.
entries.example: IP targets in awsvpc ECS mode.

blocks.text: Wrong load balancer choice breaks features: NLB cannot route on URL path; ALB cannot raw TCP game servers efficiently. PrivateLink provider services require NLB. GWLB is the interview answer for centralized IDS/IPS. Cross-zone load balancing and connection draining differ by type.

blocks.title: Quick pick
blocks.body: HTTP/API → ALB. Static IP / TCP / PrivateLink → NLB. Inline security appliances → GWLB.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

diagram.title: Three load balancer layers
diagram.source:
flowchart TB
  Client[Client] --> ALB[ALB L7 HTTP]
  Client --> NLB[NLB L4 TCP/UDP]
  Client --> GWLB[GWLB L3 inspection]
  ALB --> App1[ECS HTTP targets]
  NLB --> App2[TCP targets / PrivateLink]
  GWLB --> FW[Firewall appliance]
  FW --> App3[Protected subnets]

snippet.label: CloudFormation — ALB with path rule
snippet.code:
AlbListenerRule:
  Type: AWS::ElasticLoadBalancingV2::ListenerRule
  Properties:
    ListenerArn: !Ref HttpsListener
    Priority: 10
    Conditions:
      - Field: path-pattern
        Values: ["/api/*"]
    Actions:
      - Type: forward
        TargetGroupArn: !Ref ApiTargetGroup
snippet.explanation: ALB content-based routing — impossible on NLB without TLS SNI tricks.

snippet.label: CloudFormation — NLB with static EIP
snippet.code:
NlbEipAzA:
  Type: AWS::EC2::EIP

Nlb:
  Type: AWS::ElasticLoadBalancingV2::LoadBalancer
  Properties:
    Type: network
    Scheme: internet-facing
    SubnetMappings:
      - SubnetId: !Ref PublicSubnetA
        AllocationId: !GetAtt NlbEipAzA.AllocationId
snippet.explanation: NLB SubnetMappings with AllocationId provide static IPs for allow-list integrations.

snippet.label: CLI — create GWLB
snippet.code:
aws elbv2 create-load-balancer \
  --name sec-gwlb \
  --type gateway \
  --subnet-mappings SubnetId=subnet-private-a

aws elbv2 create-target-group \
  --name firewall-tg \
  --protocol GENEVE \
  --port 6081 \
  --vpc-id vpc-0abc \
  --target-type ip
snippet.explanation: GWLB uses GENEVE protocol on port 6081 to appliance targets.

snippet.label: CLI — ALB target health
snippet.explanation: Unhealthy targets with healthy app often implicates security group — ALB SG must reach target port.

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: ALB for raw TCP database — use NLB. NLB for URL-based microservice routing — use ALB. Forgetting NLB preserves IP but target SG sees client IP only with preserve_client_ip enabled on target group.

blocks.text: ALB supports connection idle timeout and HTTP desync mitigation modes. NLB cross-zone incurs charges but improves even distribution. GWLB integrates via VPC route tables pointing to GWLB endpoint — appliances see encapsulated flows. How to prove it in production: ALB access logs; NLB TCP reset metrics; GWLB appliance metrics on dropped GENEVE packets.

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Saying ALB and NLB are interchangeable. Strong answer: L7 vs L4; NLB for PrivateLink provider and static IP; GWLB for inline security appliances.

interviewTakeaways: ALB = Layer 7 HTTP/HTTPS routing and WAF integration.
NLB = Layer 4 TCP/UDP, static IPs, PrivateLink provider requirement, extreme scale.
GWLB = Layer 3 transparent traffic inspection via GENEVE appliances.
60s: HTTP → ALB. TCP/static IP/PrivateLink → NLB. Firewall inline → GWLB. Match OSI layer to choice.
Follow-up: why must PrivateLink provider use NLB not ALB?
commonPitfalls: Using ALB for PrivateLink provider service — rejected; PrivateLink requires NLB (or GWLB for specific cases).
Strong answer: NLB for provider; ALB for HTTP consumer-facing APIs.
Target SG allows 0.0.0.0/0 instead of ALB SG reference.
GWLB route table mispoint — traffic bypasses inspection silently.

jsTsCorrelations.note: ALB sets X-Forwarded-For; Node trust proxy config matters for rate limits — NLB TCP pass-through has no such headers unless TLS terminates elsewhere.
TypeScript Socket.io works on ALB with sticky sessions or shared Redis — NLB passes TCP but no HTTP stickiness without client IP affinity.
